content.text: LESSON
Rates of reaction
Year 11 · Chemistry
By the end of this lesson I can
measure reaction rate from experimental data and calculate mean rates and instantaneous rates from graphs.
explain the effects of concentration, gas pressure, temperature and surface area using collision theory.
explain how catalysts increase reaction rate using activation energy and reaction profiles.
Do now
STARTER
In the particle model, how do particles in a liquid move?
Randomly
What unit could you use to measure the volume of a gas?
cm³
On a graph showing change over time, which axis usually shows time?
The x-axis

slides.notes:
1. Particles in a liquid move randomly. This is part of the particle model; we will build on it when we consider collisions. 2. Gas volume can be measured in cubic centimetres (cm³). This gives us a unit for the gas produced in the reaction. 3. Time usually goes on the x-axis. This lets us track how a measured quantity changes over time.
Answers: 1. Randomly 2. cm³ 3. The x-axis

content.text: Gas production reveals reaction rate
Marble reaction:
Collect the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe. Record its volume at intervals.
Rate:
Measure product formed per unit time. Gas volume is measured in cm³/s.
Graph:
The gradient is the change in gas volume divided by the time taken. A steeper gradient means more gas forms each second; a tangent gives the rate at one instant.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Carbon dioxide volume rises to 60 cubic centimetres at 30 seconds, then stays constant; a tangent touches the curve at 10 seconds.

slides.notes: Our marble chips produce carbon dioxide as they react with excess hydrochloric acid. Excess means there is more acid than the marble needs, so the marble runs out first. Connect the flask to a gas syringe, check for leaks and start recording as the reactants meet. A balance is an alternative: escaping carbon dioxide causes mass loss. Rate describes how quickly the change happens, not just how much gas is eventually made. Point to the steep early section and the flat final section. To find a rate at one instant, draw a tangent that follows the curve's direction at that point, then calculate its gradient. This graph shows illustrative experimental data.

content.text: Calculating reaction rates
What are the mean rate over 30 s and the rate at 10 s for the marble reaction?
WORKING
Mean rate = quantity change ÷ time — use the whole interval
60 − 0 = 60 cm³ — find the gas volume change
60 ÷ 30 = 2 cm³/s — the mean rate over 30 s
Tangent rise = 60 − 10 = 50 cm³ — use two points on the tangent
Tangent run = 20 − 0 = 20 s — use those points' times
50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 cm³/s — the instantaneous rate at 10 s
WORKED EXAMPLE

slides.notes: Show the first line, then ask the class to supply each later line before revealing it. For the mean rate, the volume change is 60 − 0 = 60 cm³, so 60 ÷ 30 = 2 cm³/s. For the instantaneous rate, use the tangent rather than two points on the reaction curve. Its rise is 60 − 10 = 50 cm³ and its run is 20 − 0 = 20 s, giving 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 cm³/s. Choose well-separated points on the tangent to reduce reading error. Explain that a mean smooths out the changing rate, whereas an instantaneous rate describes one moment. A mass-loss calculation uses the same method with grams.

content.text: Quick check
CHECK
How can you measure the carbon dioxide made?
Use a gas syringe; record volume over time.
What does a steeper gradient show?
A faster rate.
What are the mean rate and rate at 10 s?
2 cm³/s mean; 2.5 cm³/s at 10 s.

slides.notes:
Answers: 1. Collect the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe and record its volume at intervals; divide the gas volume change by the time taken to find the rate in cm³/s. 2. A steeper gradient means a faster rate; the gradient of a tangent gives the rate at that instant. If pupils say the curve’s height gives the rate, revisit the difference between volume and gradient. 3. The mean rate is 2 cm³/s and the rate at 10 s is 2.5 cm³/s. For the mean, 60 cm³ ÷ 30 s = 2 cm³/s. For the tangent, (60 − 10) cm³ ÷ (20 − 0) s = 2.5 cm³/s. If pupils use 60 ÷ 10, remind them that the instantaneous rate comes from the tangent’s rise divided by its run, not the total volume divided by the time shown.
Answers: 1. Use a gas syringe; record volume over time. 2. A faster rate. 3. 2 cm³/s mean; 2.5 cm³/s at 10 s.

content.text: Successful collisions control reaction rate
Marble reaction:
More concentrated acid produces carbon dioxide faster. More acid particles collide with the marble each second.
Collision theory:
Reacting particles must collide with enough energy. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction.
Other factors:
Higher gas pressure or greater solid surface area increases collision frequency. Higher temperature increases the proportion of collisions with enough energy.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: A table links increased concentration, gas pressure, surface area and temperature to changes in particle collisions.

slides.notes: Collision theory explains a reaction through the behaviour of particles. Collisions below the activation energy do not cause a reaction. Increasing concentration puts more dissolved reacting particles into the same volume. Increasing pressure compresses reacting gases: this explanation applies to gases, not to marble chips in acid. Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more particles without changing its mass. Heating increases particles' kinetic energy, the energy of movement. They move faster and collide more often, but the crucial extra effect is that a greater proportion of collisions reaches the activation energy. Heating does not lower that energy barrier.

content.text: Explaining a faster reaction
Why does powdered marble react faster than equal-mass chips with the same excess acid?
WORKING
Same marble mass and excess acid — only the surface area changes
Powder has more exposed surface — acid reaches more marble particles
More collisions happen each second — more particles can react
More successful collisions form gas faster — the same marble mass gives the same final gas volume
WORKED EXAMPLE

slides.notes: Reveal the first line and ask the class for each later line before showing it. Both experiments use the same marble mass, acid concentration, acid volume and temperature. Powder has a larger total exposed surface area, so acid particles can reach more marble particles at once. There are more collisions per second and therefore more successful collisions per second. The reaction is faster, but the same amount of marble produces the same final gas volume because acid remains in excess. Powder does not lower activation energy. Ask pupils to rehearse the explanation using surface area, collision frequency and successful collisions.

content.text: Quick check
CHECK
Why does more concentrated acid produce carbon dioxide faster?
More particles per unit volume cause more frequent collisions.
What must be true for a collision to cause a reaction?
It must have at least the activation energy.
Why does powdered marble react faster than equal-mass chips?
It has more exposed surface, causing more frequent collisions.

slides.notes:
The answers are: 1. More concentrated acid has more particles per unit volume, so particles collide with the marble more often each second. 2. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction; a collision must have at least this much energy to react. 3. Powdered marble has more exposed surface, so acid particles collide with it more often. More successful collisions form carbon dioxide faster, but the same marble mass gives the same final gas volume. If pupils say that every collision reacts, revisit the rule that collisions need enough energy. If they say higher temperature only makes collisions more frequent, return to the table: it also increases the proportion of collisions with enough energy.
Answers: 1. More particles per unit volume cause more frequent collisions. 2. It must have at least the activation energy. 3. It has more exposed surface, causing more frequent collisions.

content.text: Catalysts lower activation energy
Hydrogen peroxide:
Manganese dioxide speeds its breakdown into water and oxygen. The catalyst is not used up.
Alternative route:
A catalyst gives the reaction a route with lower activation energy. At the same temperature, more collisions have enough energy to react.
Reaction profile:
Activation energy is the rise from the reactants to the peak. Reactant and product energies stay unchanged.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Two reaction pathways start and finish at the same energy; the catalysed pathway has a lower peak.

slides.notes: The vertical scale is illustrative relative energy, not measured data. Trace each route from the same reactant energy. Activation energy is measured from the reactants to the peak, not from zero. The uncatalysed barrier is 100 − 40 = 60 relative units; the catalysed barrier is 60 − 40 = 20 relative units. The catalyst changes the pathway, not the reactant or product energies, so the overall energy change is unchanged. Different reactions need different catalysts. Manganese dioxide is a catalyst for hydrogen peroxide decomposition; do not assume it catalyses the marble reaction.

content.text: Explaining catalyst action
Why does manganese dioxide produce oxygen faster from hydrogen peroxide at the same temperature?
WORKING
Manganese dioxide provides another pathway — it acts as a catalyst
The pathway has lower activation energy — the energy barrier is smaller
More collisions meet the energy requirement — the temperature is unchanged
Oxygen forms faster — the catalyst is not used up overall
WORKED EXAMPLE

slides.notes: Show the first line, then ask the class to predict each later line before revealing it. Keep temperature and the amount and concentration of hydrogen peroxide unchanged. The explanation must connect an alternative pathway to lower activation energy, then to more successful collisions per second. The catalyst does not make particles hotter. It may take part in intermediate steps, but it is regenerated and is not used up overall. For a fixed amount of hydrogen peroxide undergoing complete decomposition, it changes how quickly oxygen forms, not the final amount.

content.text: What does heating increase that a catalyst lowers?
Particles' kinetic energy
Activation energy
Neither of these
Both of these

slides.notes:
Heating increases particles' kinetic energy, whereas a catalyst lowers activation energy.
Neither of these is correct: heating increases particles' kinetic energy, but a catalyst does not lower it; a catalyst lowers activation energy, but heating does not increase it. Choosing particles' kinetic energy suggests the pupil thinks catalysts slow particles down. Choosing activation energy suggests the pupil thinks heating raises the energy barrier. Choosing both conflates the energy particles have with the energy they need. Revisit the collision table and reaction profile if either energy is confused before pupils work independently.

content.text: Your turn: explain reaction rates
PRACTICE
Show your working or write a short explanation.
1: A reaction loses 1.8 g in 60 s; calculate its mean rate.
2: A tangent rises from 12 to 42 cm³ between 4 and 14 s; calculate the instantaneous rate.
3: A catalyst is said to heat particles; correct this using activation energy.
4: Our 60 cm³ marble reaction now finishes in 15 s with powder; calculate its mean rate and explain the unchanged final volume.

slides.notes: 1: Mean rate = 1.8 ÷ 60 = 0.03 g/s. 2: Rise = 42 − 12 = 30 cm³; run = 14 − 4 = 10 s; instantaneous rate = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 cm³/s. 3: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful at the same temperature; it does not heat the particles. 4: Mean rate = 60 ÷ 15 = 4 cm³/s. The original mean rate was 60 ÷ 30 = 2 cm³/s. Powder exposes a greater surface area, increasing collision frequency and successful collisions per second. Equal marble mass with excess acid produces the same final 60 cm³: rate changes, not the amount available to react. This settles our opening marble case. Harder challenge: the same gas reaction gives 48 cm³ after 12 s and 72 cm³ after 24 s; compare its mean rate in this interval with 4 cm³/s and explain why the comparison is not an instantaneous rate. Volume change = 72 − 48 = 24 cm³; time change = 24 − 12 = 12 s; mean rate = 24 ÷ 12 = 2 cm³/s. It is half of 4 cm³/s and averages a whole interval rather than using a tangent at one instant.

misconceptions.belief: A faster reaction means particles collide more often, regardless of their energy. In fact, reaction requires successful collisions: particles must collide with at least the activation energy, and temperature also changes the proportion of collisions that meet this requirement.
